deep.reconstruction:
PROBLEM (Gauss's heading): the 'inverse problem'. Given the orthogonal projection of a planetary (Keplerian) ellipse together with the projection of its focus, recover the true orbit: semi-axis a, eccentricity e, node Ω, inclination i, and E. E is evidently the angle of perihelion from the node, i.e. the argument of perihelion ω.

DATA. The projected ellipse has semi-axes α and β. The transcription's '6' is β. Angles are measured from the centre against an arbitrary abscissa line:
- P is the direction of α.
- Q is the direction of the line from the centre to the projected focus, whose length is δ.

STEP 1 (conjugate diameter). Define R by tan(R−P)·tan(Q−P) = −β²/α². This is the condition for the diameters in directions Q and R to be conjugate in the projected ellipse.

STEP 2 (semi-diameters). The semi-diameters in these directions are q and r:
- 1/q² = cos²(Q−P)/α² + sin²(Q−P)/β²
- 1/r² = cos²(R−P)/α² + sin²(R−P)/β²

Hence q²/r² = −sin2(R−P)/sin2(Q−P). [Check, mine: with u = Q−P, v = R−P and k = β²/α², both sides equal k·cos²v/sin²u.]

STEP 3 (eccentricity). Parallel projection preserves the centre, conjugacy and ratios along a line. So the projected major axis of the true orbit is the diameter through the projected focus, with semi-length q. The focus divides it at distance ae from the centre, so e = δ/q. Gauss first wrote e = √(1−δ²/q²) and struck it out. The conjugate diameter R is the image of the minor axis b = a√(1−e²). Therefore r/√(1−e²) is the image of a vector of length a along the minor-axis direction.

STEP 4 (projection equations). Measure angles in the projection plane from the node line Ω, and let c = cos i. The perihelion unit vector (cos E, sin E) in the orbit plane projects to (cos E, c·sin E). The minor-axis direction (−sin E, cos E) projects to (−sin E, c·cos E). Hence, with s = r/√(1−e²):
- q·cos(Q−Ω) = a·cos E
- q·sin(Q−Ω) = a·cos i·sin E
- s·cos(R−Ω) = −a·sin E
- s·sin(R−Ω) = a·cos i·cos E

These four quantities are, in a node-rotated frame, what are now called Thiele–Innes constants.

STEP 5 (consequences, by sums of squares and cross/dot products).
- (a) q² + s² = a²(1+cos²i)
- (b) q·s·sin(R−Q) = a²·cos i (cross product)
- (c) q·s·cos(R−Q) = −½a²·sin²i·sin2E (dot product)
- (d) q² − s² = a²·sin²i·cos2E

Gauss also gives (1−e²)q²/r² = −sin2(R−Ω)/sin2(Q−Ω), i.e. q²·sin2(Q−Ω) + s²·sin2(R−Ω) = 0. This is the analogue of Step 2 for the projected circle of radius a.

STEP 6 (margin).
- a²sin²i·cos(Q+R−2Ω) = (q²+s²)·cos(R−Q)
- a²sin²i·sin(Q+R−2Ω) = (q²−s²)·sin(R−Q)

[Justification, mine: put z1 = q·e^{i(Q−Ω)} = a(cosE + i·c·sinE) and z2 = s·e^{i(R−Ω)} = a(−sinE + i·c·cosE). Then z1² + z2² = a²(1−c²) = a²sin²i, which is real. Multiplying by e^{−i(Q+R−2Ω)} and separating real and imaginary parts gives both margin formulas. The imaginary part of z1² + z2² = a²sin²i is the sin2 relation above.]

USE (solution scheme, implicit). From α, β, P, Q, δ compute R, q, r and e = δ/q, hence s. Q+R−2Ω then follows from the margin formulas (its tangent is ((q²−s²)/(q²+s²))·tan(R−Q)), which gives Ω. a²sin²i is then known, and (b) gives a²cos i. Together these give a and i. (c) and (d) give E = ω. The orbit is thus fully determined, up to the inherent ambiguities: sign of i, and Ω modulo 180°.
errors: No mathematical errors found. Every displayed relation checks symbolically, and the margin pair was also checked numerically (i=60°, E=30°).
The struck-out e = √(1−δ²/q²) was wrong and Gauss corrected it to e = δ/q.

Minor: the step from tan(R−P)tan(Q−P) = −β²/α² to q²/r² = −sin2(R−P)/sin2(Q−P) is stated without proof. The geometric fact that the projected focus lies on the image of the major axis at ratio e is used tacitly. Both are correct.
In the cos(R−Q) line a 'sin' is overwritten ('sin.2E'). The intended reading −½a²sin²i·sin2E is the correct one.

results.what: Conjugate-diameter relations in an ellipse: tan(R−P)tan(Q−P) = −β²/α² and q²/r² = −sin2(R−P)/sin2(Q−P)
Determination of a true Keplerian orbit from its orthogonal projection and the projected focus: e = δ/q from the diameter through the projected focus, and its conjugate as image of the minor axis
results.modern_name: Apparent-orbit to true-orbit reduction (visual binary orbit determination; methods of Savary, Encke, Herschel, Kowalsky, Glasenapp)
results.usually_credited_to: Savary (1827/30), Encke (1832), J. Herschel (1833); analytic conjugate-diameter/conic methods Kowalsky (1873), Glasenapp (1889)

results.what: Projection equations q cos(Q−Ω) = a cos ω, q sin(Q−Ω) = a cos i sin ω, s cos(R−Ω) = −a sin ω, s sin(R−Ω) = a cos i cos ω
results.modern_name: Thiele–Innes constants (in a frame rotated to the node)

results.what: Invariant relations q²+s² = a²(1+cos²i), qs sin(R−Q) = a² cos i, q²e^{2i(Q−Ω)} + s²e^{2i(R−Ω)} = a² sin²i, and the margin formulas giving Ω and a² sin²i
results.modern_name: Apollonius-type invariants of a projected circle/ellipse used to invert the projection
results.usually_credited_to: standard in later binary-star orbit theory (19th c.)

deep.surprise_reason: The page contains a complete, clean analytic solution of the problem of recovering a true Kepler orbit from its projected ellipse and projected focus. It uses conjugate diameters and quantities equivalent to (node-rotated) Thiele–Innes constants. The bundle label suggests c.1809, which would predate Savary's 1827 first binary-orbit computation and the later classical methods of Kowalsky, Glasenapp and Thiele–Innes. The mathematics is elementary for Gauss, the dating is uncertain, and the problem is posed for planetary orbits rather than binaries. Such a solution would be a notable but not major unpublished item; it may already be noted in Werke commentary (unsure).

transcription_corrections: '6' and '66' should be β and ββ (the half minor axis of the projected ellipse), not the digit 6.
In the struck-out line the content is unclear; it ends in 'qq' and seems to be an abandoned expression for e, likely e = √(1−δδ/qq), before the correct e = δ/q.
'q sin(Q−Ω) = a cos i . sin E': 'sin' is written over another word; the reading is correct.
Last relation in the column: '−½aa sin i² sin 2E', where 'sin2E' is written over an earlier 'sin E'.
E here denotes the argument of perihelion (angle from the node), not the eccentric anomaly.
The character transcribed as Ω is Gauss's node symbol (Drachenkopf ☊).
